metadata.title: From asking to observing. Behavioural measures of socio-emotional and motivational skills in large-scale assessments

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA microdata (primarily PISA 2012) and applies PISA sampling and replication weights “in line with recommended PISA procedures (OECD, 2014)”. The analytic samples are restricted to students with non-missing values for the behavioural PSEC indicators and the relevant control variables in each model specification, and for some indicators additional item-level eligibility rules are applied (e.g., dropping conditional items for non-response; requiring at least 3 non-missing items within a scale for inconsistency/non-differentiation). For the test-based behavioural indicator of performance decline, the model is estimated separately by country and standard errors are clustered at the school level to reflect the clustered sampling structure. The paper does not report the exact weight variable names in the excerpt, but it explicitly states that sampling and replication weights were used, so estimates are intended to be population-representative within the PISA design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not describe a specific missing-data handling method for the PSEC indicators and controls beyond stating that models include students with non-missing values for all PSEC indicators and control variables. This is consistent with a complete-case restriction, but the authors do not explicitly label it as listwise deletion or another formal missing-data procedure. Because the study relies on multiple questionnaire and test-derived indicators, the absence of a clearly documented missing-data strategy is a reporting gap that affects reproducibility and interpretation of selection bias.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Primary analyses are based on PISA 2012. For questionnaire-based behavioural indicators, the authors construct item non-response using only applicable items (dropping items conditional on prior items), and inconsistency/non-differentiation are computed using only respondents with non-missing responses for at least 3 items within a scale/item set (and for non-differentiation, item sets with at least 4 items). For the achievement-relationship models, they include students with non-missing values for all PSEC indicators and the control variables to ensure comparability across specifications. For the longitudinal predictive validity analyses, the sample is restricted to the subset of countries with linkable follow-up data (Denmark, Switzerland, Australia, Canada) and uses PISA at age 15 linked to completion outcomes by age 25; Table 4/5 report country-specific analytic Ns for these longitudinal models.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 (15-year-olds) — Reading, Mathematics, Science, Collaborative problem-solving
main_findings.target_variable: PSEC indicators association with contemporaneous achievement
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 3 (linear models): e.g., Non-response (Model B) b=-0.27*** (Reading), -0.26*** (Math), -0.27*** (Science), -0.27*** (Collaborative problem-solving); Adjusted R-squared ranges shown per domain (e.g., Reading Model B: 0.33; Math Model B: 0.33; Science Model B: 0.33; Collaborative problem-solving Model B: 0.19).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 the study leveraged self-reported perseverance/effort and behavioural PSEC indicators (notably non-response, non-differentiation, and inconsistency) to predict contemporaneous achievement in reading, mathematics, science, and collaborative problem-solving, finding that all PSEC indicators were negatively associated with achievement and that non-response showed the strongest relationship (e.g., Model B b≈-0.27 to -0.26 across domains). This indicates that behavioural engagement/effort markers captured during low-stakes testing provide meaningful additional information for interpreting achievement differences, even after accounting for background controls and self-reported PSEC.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 (15-year-olds) — PSEC indicators by student background (gender, SES, immigrant background)
main_findings.target_variable: Differences in PSEC indicators across student subgroups
main_findings.performance_metrics: Effect sizes reported in text (d): gender—self-reported lack of perseverance d=0.03; behavioural indicators show females better (e.g., inconsistency d=-0.11, non-response d=-0.11, undifferentiated responses d=-0.19, performance decline d=-0.07, response time effort d=-0.12). SES—self-reported lack of perseverance d=-0.28; behavioural gaps smaller (e.g., non-response d=-0.019, non-differentiation d=-0.07, inconsistency d=-0.11, performance decline d=-0.09, response time effort d=-0.012). Immigrant background—self-reported lack of perseverance d=-0.03; behavioural indicators higher for non-immigrant vs immigrant (e.g., non-response d=0.18, inconsistency d=0.17, performance decline d=0.06, response time effort d=0.27).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 the study leveraged gender, socioeconomic status, and immigrant background to predict subgroup differences in behavioural and self-reported PSEC indicators, finding that behavioural measures show clearer patterns (e.g., females lower behavioural PSEC z-scores; SES and immigrant gaps are smaller in behavioural indicators than in self-reports). This indicates that self-reports may partly reflect subjective judgments shaped by subgroup context, while behavioural indicators may better capture differences in test-taking engagement relevant for monitoring equity.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000/2003 linked follow-ups — Denmark (PISA 2000→PIAAC 2012), Switzerland (PISA 2000→TREE 2010), Australia (PISA 2003→LSAY 2013), Canada (PISA 2000→YITS 2010)
main_findings.target_variable: Predictive validity of PSEC indicators for education completion by age 25
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 4: Performance decline—University completion b=-0.066 (Denmark, not significant), b=-0.074*** (Switzerland), b=-0.070* (Australia), b=-0.132*** (Canada); Adjusted R-squared: Denmark 0.148, Switzerland 0.125, Australia 0.205, Canada 0.20. Table 4 also reports Inconsistency/Non-response/Non-differentiation coefficients with significance varying by country (e.g., Non-response—University b=-0.072*** in Canada; Non-response—Upper secondary b=-0.053* in Denmark). Table 5 incremental power: Performance decline—University b=-0.071*** (Switzerland) and b=-0.072* (Australia) and b=-0.059 (Denmark) with adjusted R-squared improvements shown.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using linked PISA follow-up data for Denmark, Switzerland, Australia, and Canada, the study leveraged behavioural PSEC indicators—especially performance decline—along with self-reported perseverance/effort controls to predict education completion by age 25, finding that performance decline was associated with lower university completion in most countries and showed the strongest incremental predictive power in models that account for self-reported PSEC. This indicates that behavioural engagement measures from low-stakes assessments can support early identification of students at risk of weaker long-term educational attainment, informing longitudinal monitoring and targeted support, while causality cannot be inferred from these observational links.

data.outcome_summary: This study develops and validates behavioural measures of socio-emotional and motivational skills (PSEC) using PISA microdata, primarily PISA 2012, and compares them with self-reported PSEC indicators. It constructs behavioural indicators from questionnaire responses (item non-response, inconsistency, non-differentiation) and from test-taking behaviour (performance decline and, for a subset of countries, response time effort from computer-based log files). Across countries, behavioural and self-reported measures show weak-to-moderate convergence, but behavioural indicators are consistently negatively associated with contemporaneous achievement in reading, mathematics, science, and collaborative problem-solving (Table 3), with non-response showing the strongest relationship. For a longitudinal subset of Denmark, Switzerland, Australia, and Canada, performance decline predicts lower university completion by age 25 and retains significance after controlling for self-reported PSEC (Tables 4–5). The paper does not document a formal missing-data procedure beyond restricting to non-missing cases, and the evidence is correlational/observational rather than causal.
